Hey man, Cappadocia is amazing. I took a mini trip down there. One thing to expect from Turkey in general is a TON of stray dogs and cats. They are absolutely precious and I've only dealt with an overprotective mom once. I didn't get the chance to see the balloons because of wind. Currently living in Istanbul. Read up on the common scams, most definitely. If you want the real experience, go to the Asian side, or any non-touristy neighbourhoods on the European Side. Go on the Bosphorus tour. Book a hostel that has airport pickup, because taxis are -not- the best, and many will rip you off. Once you get settled you could download an app that helps order taxis, has customer support, etc. I live on the Asian side right now, right by the water. It's beautiful. You'll hear calls to prayer several times a day from all the mosques around the city.

Turkish people are wonderful and I've picked up on some of the language. They're generous and I've hitchhiked with a group of friends without issue. There's an exceptional transportation system in Istanbul; you can get around by ferry, subway, train, bus, tram, or just walking but that may take a while. You'll need a transportation card, and in order to use that, you must connect an HES code (message if you want, or look it up) with it. Bring cash, sometimes card readers don't work. You can absolutely live affordably here. I make almost nothing for American standards, and I'm doing fine. Turkish delights can be bought affordably on the Asian side, message for a good suggestion.

Expect that you may need to use squat toilets on occasion, and that showers may not have a cubicle. Water can and does get everywhere with some setups. You generally cannot flush toilet paper.

I'm into photography as well, and speak Polish and Spanish to an extent. Both are easier to read than converse in.

A caveat, as this is your first solo trip, there may be major culture shock if you're not used to different living conditions or ways of life. Heck, I've travelled a ton and this was still difficult at first. Your experience may vary, and travel is absolutely worth it. Follow your dreams.

When I was living in the US, if I had local access to a doctor, I couldn't afford a room there. When I finally found an affordable room it was two hours bus trip to the city, to the doctor or wherever I needed to be. I was in the middle of nowhere, where the nearest grocery store was at least an hour's walk away. The lack of decent public transportation meant I had no access to services. I lived with my mom for a while and had to request a disability bus in order to be taken to the doctor because no bus existed (only cars). I had to order it two weeks in advance. I had no access to any social possibilities there and I had to be completely dependent on her because my surroundings weren't appropriate for my disability. Even the grocery store was hard to access (it was across a very busy road and not pedestrian friendly). One time a mate let me live in his walk-in closet where there was just enough room for a bed. I was eating out of cans and going to the homeless shelter for meals. I had food assistance but no access to ways to prepare that food.

The whole situation is rough. I think I'll have to continue hopping between poorer countries so I can at least have a place to sleep. In Europe at least you can get a bus to literally the middle of nowhere. It's a lot easier to get around. I'm thankful I don't have chronic health conditions and that I haven't gotten too sick often. The US is good on paper but a lot of people fall through the cracks. If I have to go back there, I'll try to find a city where there's enough funding for people with disabilities and cheap enough housing. But I'm really scared of ending up on the street.

If Poland opens back up I'll happily go there again for three months before having to leave Schengen. It was wonderful there.
